segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he began to speak to them in parables:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “A man planted a vineyard, put a fence around it, dug a vat for the winepress, and built a watchtower. Then he leased it to tenants and went abroad.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: When the season came, he sent a slave to the tenants to collect from them some of the fruit of the vineyard.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But they took him, beat him, and sent him away empty-handed.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Again he sent another slave to them; that one they struck on the head and treated shamefully.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He sent another, and that one they killed; and so with many others, beating some and killing others.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He still had one, a beloved son. He sent him to them last, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But those tenants said to one another, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So they took him and killed him, and threw him out of the vineyard.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: What will the owner of the vineyard do? He will come and destroy the tenants and give the vineyard to others.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Have you not even read this Scripture: ‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: this came from the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes’?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they were looking for a way to arrest him, but they feared the crowd, for they knew that he had told the parable against them. So they left him and went away.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then they sent some of the Pharisees and the Herodians to him, to trap him in something he said.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They came and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and are swayed by no one, for you pay no regard to people’s standing but truly teach the way of God. Is it lawful to pay the tax to Caesar or not? Should we pay, or should we not pay?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he, knowing their hypocrisy, said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Why are you testing me? Bring me a denarius so that I can look at it.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They brought one. And he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Whose image is this, and whose inscription?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Caesar’s.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Give back to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they were utterly amazed at him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then some Sadducees, who say there is no resurrection, came to him and put a question to him:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man’s brother dies and leaves a wife behind but leaves no child, the man is to take the wife and raise up offspring for his brother.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: There were seven brothers. The first took a wife, and when he died he left no offspring.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: The second took her and died, leaving no offspring behind, and the third likewise.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: None of the seven left offspring. Last of all, the woman died too.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: In the resurrection, when they rise, whose wife will she be? For all seven had her as wife.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Is this not why you are mistaken: you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For when they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in the heavens.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And as for the dead being raised, have you not read in the book of Moses, in the passage about the bush, how God spoke to him, saying, ‘I am the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob’?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He is not God of the dead but of the living. You are badly mistaken.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: One of the scribes came up and heard them debating. Seeing that Jesus had answered them well, he asked him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Which commandment is first of all?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “The first is, ‘Hear, Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The second is this: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ There is no other commandment greater than these.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the scribe said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Well said, Teacher. You have truly said that he is one, and there is no other besides him;

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: and to love him with all one’s heart and with all one’s understanding and with all one’s strength, and to love one’s neighbor as oneself, is far more than all the whole burnt offerings and sacrifices.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus saw that he had answered thoughtfully, he said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You are not far from the kingdom of God.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And after that no one dared to question him any longer.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As Jesus was teaching in the temple, he responded by saying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “How can the scribes say that the Messiah is the son of David?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: David himself said by the Holy Spirit, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand until I put your enemies under your feet.”’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: David himself calls him ‘Lord’; so how can he be his son?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the large crowd was listening to him with delight.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And in his teaching he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Beware of the scribes, who want to walk around in long robes, and want greetings in the marketplaces

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at banquets.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: They devour widows’ houses and for show make long prayers. These will receive a more severe judgment.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He sat down opposite the treasury and watched how the crowd was putting money into the treasury. Many rich people were putting in large sums.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then one poor widow came and put in two tiny coins, which make a quadrans.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Calling his disciples to him, he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all those who are putting into the treasury.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For they all put in out of their surplus, but she, out of her poverty, put in everything she had—her whole livelihood.”

notes.note: The fence, vat, and tower echo the song of the vineyard in Isaiah 5, where the vineyard is Israel and its owner is God. A hearer who knew the Scriptures would have recognized the allusion at once and understood the tenants as those entrusted with God’s people.

The Greek word denotes a person owned by a master, not a hired employee, and first-century readers would have understood it so. Many traditional versions use “servant,” which softens the social reality; a number of modern translations now use “slave.”

This verb is extremely rare and its exact meaning is uncertain. It is evidently formed from the word for “head,” and most translators take it as “struck on the head” or “wounded in the head”; a few have suggested “dealt with summarily.”

The Greek is literally “head of the corner,” quoting Psalm 118:22. It may mean a foundation stone at the corner of a building or the capstone that completes an arch or wall. Scholars are divided; either way it is the stone on which the structure depends.

The Herodians were evidently supporters of the Herodian dynasty, which ruled by Roman favor; little else is known of them. Their pairing with the Pharisees sharpens the trap: a “no” to the tax could be reported as sedition, while a “yes” would discredit Jesus with the people.

The Greek word is borrowed from the Latin census and refers to the head tax Rome levied on Judea after it came under direct Roman rule. The tax was deeply resented and had provoked armed revolt when it was introduced. The denarius Jesus asks for was a Roman silver coin bearing the emperor’s portrait and titles.

The older English tradition has “Why tempt ye me?” The Greek verb means to put to the test, here with the aim of trapping, and “tempt” now suggests enticement to sin. Most modern translations also use “test” in this verse.

The questioners asked whether to “give” the tax; Jesus answers with a compound verb meaning to give back or pay what is owed. Traditional versions have “render,” which is accurate but now obscure, and many modern ones simply have “give.” The implication is that the coin, bearing Caesar’s image, already belongs to him.
The Greek is plural, a Semitic turn of phrase for God’s dwelling. Most translations flatten it to “heaven”; the plural is kept here because the Greek has it.

notes.phrase: in the passage about the bush
notes.note: The Greek says simply “at the bush.” Before chapter and verse numbers existed, a passage was cited by its subject; this is the account of the burning bush in Exodus 3. Jesus argues from the Law of Moses, which the Sadducees acknowledged as authoritative.
The traditional word “scribes” is kept, but these were not copyists. They were trained scholars and teachers of the Law of Moses, recognized as authorities on its interpretation.

notes.phrase: the Lord our God, the Lord is one
notes.traditional: The Lord our God is one Lord
notes.note: This is the opening of the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4), recited daily by observant Jews. The Greek, like the Hebrew behind it, can be construed in several ways: “the Lord our God is one Lord,” “the Lord our God, the Lord is one,” or “the Lord is our God, the Lord alone.” The scribe’s reply in verse 32 (“he is one”) favors the rendering chosen here.

The Greek word, traditionally “Christ,” is here a title under discussion: the anointed king Israel expected. “Messiah” conveys the title to a modern reader, for whom “Christ” sounds like a name. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels.

The quotation is from Psalm 110:1. Many manuscripts read “a footstool for your feet,” matching the Greek Old Testament; the text translated here reads “under your feet,” which is probably the earlier wording in Mark, later conformed to the psalm.

The widow’s coins were lepta, the smallest coins in circulation. Mark explains their value for his readers in Roman terms: together they equaled a quadrans, the smallest Roman coin, one sixty-fourth of a denarius, which was roughly a laborer’s daily wage.

Frequent in the Gospels and Acts; “scribe” suggests a copyist to modern readers, and alternatives such as “legal expert” or “teacher of the Law” need one consistent decision.
Recurs in controversy stories and in Paul; “lawful” versus “permitted” affects whether readers hear civil law, Torah, or general permission.

Used across the New Testament for error, deception, and straying; renderings vary among “deceive,” “lead astray,” “err,” and “be mistaken,” and the links between passages are lost if it varies freely.
Recurs in the Gospels and letters where translators alternate among “judgment,” “condemnation,” and “sentence,” with real theological consequences.
